# federation-js: Runtime Module Federation

URL: https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/federation-js

Runtime for JavaScript module federation, built on a SystemJS-style module registry.

**FynMesh:** [Website](https://www.fynmesh.fyi) · [Demo](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/demo) · [Shell demo](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/shell)

This is the piece that runs in the browser. It resolves shared modules across independently
built and deployed bundles, keeps a single instance of a shared dependency when asked to, and
lets one bundle load modules exposed by another.

Containers are normally generated for you by
[`rollup-plugin-federation`](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/rollup-plugin-federation) — you rarely construct one by hand.

## Install

```sh
npm install federation-js
```

## The module loader

federation-js is half of a pair. It does not carry a module registry of its own — it expects a
`System` global, and it must be the fork of SystemJS this package ships, not stock SystemJS.
The fork keeps the module registry, name→url, url→module and per-version qualifiers in
`System.registrations`; stock SystemJS has no such thing, and a crossed pair fails in ways that
look like federation bugs.

Both loader builds are in this package's `dist`, so load one before the runtime:

```html
<!-- development: readable, keeps the long-form diagnostics -->
<script src="/node_modules/federation-js/dist/system.js"></script>
<script src="/node_modules/federation-js/dist/federation-js.dev.js"></script>
```

```html
<!-- production -->
<script src="/node_modules/federation-js/dist/system.min.js"></script>
<script src="/node_modules/federation-js/dist/federation-js.min.js"></script>
```

Keep the two halves on the same build: `system.js` with `federation-js.dev.js`, `system.min.js`
with `federation-js.min.js`.

## Runtime

Importing the runtime installs a `Federation` instance on the global object:

```js
import "federation-js/runtime";

// load a container and pull an exposed module out of it
Federation.import("__mf_container_plugin_1")
  .then((container) => container.get("./bootstrap"))
  .then((getModule) => console.log("module", getModule()));
```

A shared module is retrieved the same way, by the name it was shared under:

```js
Federation.import("__mf_container_plugin_1")
  .then((container) => container.get("react"))
  .then((getModule) => console.log("module", getModule()));
```

A container that only *consumes* a shared module can still resolve it, provided some container
that shares it has already loaded.

### Debugging a minified page

`Federation.__I()` returns a snapshot of what the runtime decided about shared-module
resolution: for every chunk and share key, the importer-declared ranges, the ranges
resolution actually applied, and the versions this runtime's own semver accepts. It is in
the minified build too — that is the build it exists for, since the same information is
readable off `$SS` and `$SC` in a development one. The result is a versioned envelope,
`{ v: 1, r: [...] }`; check `v` before reading the rest.

The name is `__I` because nobody guesses it, which is the intent: it is a debugging hatch,
not part of the API a container or the loader talks to.

### Combined module files

Several modules can be shipped in one physical file. Each still registers itself under its own
filename, so nothing about importing it changes — the file it arrived in is not part of its
identity. A module built into a combined file carries `b` (the physical file) alongside `f`
(itself); when they differ, the runtime derives the module's own url from `f` rather than from
`document.currentScript`, which would otherwise be the same for every module in the file.

Two ways a combined file gets used:

- **Already loaded** — a plain `<script>` tag is enough. Every module in it registers, and a
  later import of any of them resolves without a request.
- **Not loaded yet** — the container entry declares which file carries which modules
  (`Federation._B(map, container, version)`), and the first import of any member pulls that file
  once, however many members ask at the same time. If the file turns out not to carry the module
  it claimed, the runtime warns and loads that module's own file instead.

Pulling a file registers its modules; it does not execute them. A module's body still runs on
first import, exactly once.

Producing these files is a build concern — see `rollup-plugin-federation`'s
`federation-combine`.

## Entry points

| Import | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `federation-js` | `Container` class and the public types |
| `federation-js/runtime` | the runtime; installs the global `Federation` |
| `federation-js/container` | `Container` on its own |
| `federation-js/types` | types on their own |

Shared-module resolution is semver aware: a container declares the range it accepts, and the
runtime picks a loaded version that satisfies it, falling back to loading its own copy when
nothing matches.

## License

Apache-2.0

---

# rollup-plugin-federation: Module Federation for Rollup

URL: https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/rollup-plugin-federation

Module federation for [Rollup](https://rollupjs.org). Build a bundle that shares modules with,
and exposes modules to, other independently built and deployed bundles.

**FynMesh:** [Website](https://www.fynmesh.fyi) · [Demo](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/demo) · [Shell demo](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/shell)

The plugin generates a *container* entry for your build: it collects the shared modules and
their importers, emits the container runtime code, and writes federation metadata describing
what the bundle exposes and shares. At runtime those containers are wired together by
[`federation-js`](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/federation-js).

## Install

```sh
npm install --save-dev rollup-plugin-federation
```

## Usage

```js
import federation from "rollup-plugin-federation";

export default {
  input: ["src/index.js", "federation-entry.js"],
  output: { dir: "dist", format: "esm" },
  plugins: [
    federation({
      name: "plugin_1",
      // must also appear in the input array above
      filename: "federation-entry.js",
      exposes: {
        "./bootstrap": "./src/bootstrap.js",
      },
      shared: {
        react: { singleton: true, semver: "^19.0.0" },
      },
    }),
  ],
};
```

`filename` names the container entry the plugin generates — **it has to be listed in Rollup's
`input` as well**, or the entry is never emitted.

## Options

| Option | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `string` | **Required.** Name of this container. |
| `filename` | `string` | **Required.** Output filename for the container entry. Also add it to `input`. |
| `exposes` | `Record<string, string>` | Modules this container exposes to others. |
| `shared` | `Record<string, SharedConfig>` | Modules shared with other containers. |
| `shareScope` | `string` | Namespace for sharing. Defaults to the built-in scope. |
| `version` | `string` | Version of this container. Defaults to the host package's version. |
| `emitFederationJson` | `boolean` | Emit federation info as JSON. Defaults to `true`. |
| `debugging` | `boolean` | Enable debug logging and output. |
| `renderDynamicImport` | `object` | Dynamic import rendering per import type. |
| `entry.header` / `entry.footer` | `string` | Code inserted at the start/end of the entry file. |
| `emitMeta`, `emitFederationMeta`, `enrichManifest` | `function` | Hooks to emit or enrich metadata. |

### Shared modules

```js
shared: {
  react: {
    singleton: true,     // only one instance across all containers
    semver: "^19.0.0",   // range this container accepts
    eager: false,        // load at startup rather than lazily
    import: true,        // bundle a copy, or treat as external
  },
}
```

A dependency consumed only *transitively* still has to appear in `shared` with its semver range
— listing it as an external alone is not enough, and a mismatch shows up at runtime as a
duplicate-instance error rather than a build failure.

## Metadata the build emits

Alongside the container entry and its chunks, the plugin writes metadata describing the
build. Two files, plus one copy embedded in the entry itself.

**`federation.json`** — a record of what this build produced: `name`, `filename`,
`shareScope`, each expose mapped to `{ path, chunks }`, each shared module's config, and a
timestamp. Emitted unless `emitFederationJson: false`, in which case the same info object is
still handed to `emitFederationMeta`.

Nothing requires it. It is build and serving metadata for your own tooling — the runtime
never needs it, since the entry file carries the container, its exposes and its shares.
`federation-combine` keeps its `bundles` record current when the file is there, but works
without it.

**An embedded manifest**, if you supply `enrichManifest`. Because dynamic imports are not
discovered until every module has been processed, the manifest cannot exist when the
container code is generated — so the entry gets a `{ __placeholder: true }` stub, and
`generateBundle` splices the enriched manifest into the emitted code afterwards, matching
both the development and minified forms. The result is exported as `__FYNAPP_MANIFEST__` and
assigned onto the container, which lets a runtime read a bundle's metadata without a second
request.

That substitution is a text patch over generated code, and a build where it fails to match
still succeeds — it warns and ships the placeholder. If a consumer of yours reads the
embedded manifest without a fallback, check for it in CI.

**Whatever `emitFederationMeta` emits.** The hook receives the federation info, the runtime,
the plugin context and the bundle, so it can emit metadata in whatever shape its consumers
want. In the [fynmesh](https://github.com/jchip/fynmesh) colorepo, this pair of hooks is what
produces a FynApp's `fynapp.manifest.json`; see
[notes/BUILD-ARTIFACTS.md](https://github.com/jchip/fynmesh/blob/main/notes/BUILD-ARTIFACTS.md)
there for a worked example of both hooks and how a runtime consumes their output.

## Combining small chunks — `federation-combine`

One chunk is emitted per expose, so a container with many small exposes ships many tiny files
whose cost is almost entirely request overhead. `federation-combine` folds them into one
physical file per group, while each module keeps its own identity and stays importable by its
own filename.

It is a **post-build step over a finished dist directory**, not part of the plugin's pipeline —
so it can be re-run with a different policy, or applied at deploy time to artifacts someone
else built.

```bash
federation-combine demo/fynapp-1/dist --dry-run
federation-combine demo/*/dist
```

```
--max-module <bytes>   only chunks at or below this size are candidates (2048)
--max-bundle <bytes>   stop adding to a group at this size (32768)
--min-group <count>    a group needs at least this many chunks (2)
--exclude <a,b>        fileNames or stems to leave in their own file
--group <name=a,b>     an explicit group, bypassing the size rules; repeatable
--drop-individual      delete the members' own files (removes the fallback)
--dry-run              report what would change, write nothing
```

### What combining leaves behind

The runtime is told which file carries which module by one statement appended to the
container entry, so an ordinary import works with no further help — a member's url resolves
to its carrier and the carrier is fetched once, however many of its members are asked for.

That statement runs when the entry runs, which is too late for anything that has to decide
*what to fetch* — a preload hint naming a member url names a file the runtime will never
request. So the map is also written out as **`federation.bundles.json`**, the map on its own:

```json
{ "combo-R7IaSAnm.js": ["hello-B9dQ6FmL.js", "getInfo-CH7m3ozA.js"] }
```

A host can read that without executing anything, and hand it to the runtime up front with
`Federation.declareBundles(map, distBase)` — which is what makes carriers known before the
first entry loads. Present only when a run actually combined something, and removed again
when one does not, so its presence is itself the signal that a dist has bundles to offer.

Nothing here needs `federation.json`: the container entry is the one file that calls
`_mfContainer`, and that call names the container and its version. An app that builds with
`emitFederationJson: false` combines exactly the same.

Or from a build script:

```js
import { combineDist } from "rollup-plugin-federation";

combineDist("dist", { groups: { startup: ["index", "react-esm-19.production"] } });
```

Explicit groups are taken exactly as given, which is how a known startup set is kept together
and a cold chunk is kept out of a hot one. Everything else is packed smallest-first.

The members' individual files are kept by default: if the map and the files ever disagree, the
runtime says so and loads the module's own file, so a stale map costs one request rather than a
broken page. `--drop-individual` removes that fallback, and makes the step non-repeatable.

Requires chunks built by this plugin version or newer — each chunk records the physical file it
lives in, which is what lets a combined module tell its own url apart from the file it arrived
in. Chunks without it are reported and left alone. Combined files carry no sourcemap; the
individual files keep theirs, so debug builds should simply not be combined.

## Also exported

`DependencyAnalyzer` and `DependencyUtils` for inspecting a build's dependency graph,
`combineDist` (above), plus the plugin's TypeScript types.

## License

Apache-2.0

# Federation Inspector: Debug Shared Modules

URL: https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/federation-inspector

A visual module browser for pages running [`@fynmesh/systemjs`](https://github.com/jchip/rollup-federation/tree/main/systemjs) and
[`federation-js`](https://github.com/jchip/rollup-federation/tree/main/federation-js). Drop one script tag next to them, get a
badge in the corner of the page, and click it for a dense panel showing every
module the loader knows, every federation container, every share scope, and
what actually resolved against what.

The same code is an ES library, so a Chrome DevTools extension can be built on
it without a rewrite.

```html
<script src="/federation-inspector.js"></script>
```

## What it answers

Things the browser's own devtools cannot tell you about a federated page:

| Question | Where |
| --- | --- |
| What is loaded, and what stage is each module in? | Modules |
| What depends on this? What does it depend on? | Modules, Graph |
| Which container owns this chunk? | Modules |
| Which versions of a container are live side by side? | Containers |
| Who shares `esm-react`, at what versions, from where? | Shares |
| Which copy did each app actually get, and does its semver range allow it? | Shares, Containers |
| **Are there two copies of a singleton in play?** | Issues |
| Which modules arrived inside a combined bundle? | Modules |
| What failed, and what else is stuck behind it? | Issues |

## Usage

### Standalone

Configuration goes on the script tag:

```html
<script src="/federation-inspector.js"
        data-corner="top-right"
        data-theme="dark"
        data-hotkey="ctrl+i"
        data-open="true"></script>
```

| Attribute | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `data-auto` | `true` | mount automatically; `false` to call `mount()` yourself |
| `data-corner` | `bottom-right` | `bottom-right`, `bottom-left`, `top-right`, `top-left` |
| `data-theme` | remembered, else `auto` | `auto`, `light`, `dark` -- setting it overrides what the panel remembers |
| `data-density` | remembered, else `normal` | `compact`, `normal`, `relaxed` text size |
| `data-hotkey` | `ctrl+shift+m` | toggle combination, or `false` for none |
| `data-open` | `false` | open the panel immediately |
| `data-launcher` | `true` | `false` hides the badge (hotkey/API only) |
| `data-poll` | `500` | live-refresh interval in ms, or `false` |

`data-theme` and `data-density` are the two attributes the panel itself can
change, and it remembers what you set. Omitting the attribute keeps the
remembered value; supplying one is an instruction and wins over it.

The panel's **Settings** menu, in the header at every width, holds the same
two choices plus the dock mode -- right, bottom, floating, fullscreen -- and
*Copy snapshot*. When the panel is too narrow for every tab the tab strip
scrolls: arrows appear at its ends, and the active tab is always brought into
view.

The bundle also installs `globalThis.FederationInspector`:

```js
FederationInspector.instance.open("shares");
FederationInspector.instance.close();
const snapshot = FederationInspector.collect();
```

### As a library

```ts
import { collect, analyse, mount } from "federation-inspector";

const snapshot = collect();      // plain JSON, no live loader objects
analyse(snapshot);               // graph, share resolution, diagnostics
const handle = mount({ open: true, corner: "top-left" });
```

Importing the library has **no side effects** — nothing is mounted, no hook is
installed, no global is written.

### Keyboard

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Ctrl+Shift+M` | toggle the panel |
| `Esc` | close the settings menu, then clear the filter, then close |
| `[` / `]` | previous / next tab |
| `←` / `→`, `Home` / `End` | move between tabs while one has focus |
| `j` / `k`, arrows | move the row cursor |
| `Enter` | expand the selected row |

### The graph

| Gesture | Action |
| --- | --- |
| drag | pan the canvas |
| `Ctrl`/`Cmd` + wheel, trackpad pinch | zoom about the pointer |
| wheel | scroll |
| click a node | focus its neighbourhood (a beat later, see below) |
| double-click a node | open it in Modules |
| `−` / `%` / `+` | zoom out, reset to 100%, zoom in |

Focusing a node re-lays out the graph around it, which moves the node you just
clicked -- so the click waits one double-click interval before it acts. That is
the price of keeping both gestures on the same target: without the pause the
second click of a double-click landed on empty canvas, because the first click
had already slid the node out from under the pointer.

Layout is [ELK](https://github.com/kieler/elkjs)'s layered algorithm —
crossing minimisation and orthogonal edge routing — bundled into the drop-in,
not fetched. It runs once per *shape*: the panel re-collects every 500ms, and a
graph that re-laid-out on each pass would move under you while you read it. A
module changing stage therefore redraws in place. Until the first layout
resolves (and if it ever fails) the view falls back to the built-in layered
placement, which is instant and unrouted.

### Filter grammar

The search box is the single source of filter state, so any view can be
reproduced from one string:

```
esm-react              fuzzy match on id + url
container:fynapp-1     stage:errored     kind:exposed
scope:fynmesh          share:esm-react   version:19
bundle:true            orphan:true       error:true
deps:>3                dependents:>=1
id:<full or part>      url:<full or part>
-stage:executed        any term negates with a leading "-"
```

`id:` and `url:` match alike — a case-insensitive substring — so half of an id
finds the module you half-remember. Deep links write the whole id, which no
other module's id contains, so they still land on the one module.

## How it reads the page

Read-only, and non-invasive by default. It installs no loader hook, mutates no
record, and calls no federation method that could load or resolve anything.

Its sources are:

- **`@fynmesh/systemjs`'s Record Exposure API** — `System.records`,
  `System.aliases`, `System.registrations`, `System.stageOf`. Documented,
  stable, and the reason this tool needs no cooperation from the page.
- **`Federation.$SS`** — the share store: scope → key → version → providers.
- **Container objects**, reached through the loader rather than through
  federation's own registry (see below), for `$E` (exposes), `$SC` (share
  config with the requested semver ranges), and `__FYNAPP_MANIFEST__` where a
  FynMesh build supplies one.

### Working with a minified federation build

`federation-js` ships terser-minified with property mangling, and the mangling
is not uniform. Measured against the shipped `federation-js.min.js`: `$SS`,
`$SC`, `$E` and the `_mf*` methods survive; `$C` — the runtime's container
registry — and `_mfGetContainer` do not.

So containers are enumerated from the **loader**, not the runtime. federation
files every container under a deterministic id (`__mf_container_<name>`,
qualified by version) and `System.registrations` holds it with its entry url;
the record for that url exports the live `Container`, because every generated
container entry does `exports({ container, get, init })`.

Anything still unreadable is reported as a capability note in a banner at the
top of the panel, rather than silently rendering an empty table. With no
federation on the page at all, it is a perfectly good SystemJS module browser.

### Live refresh

While open, the panel re-collects every 500ms behind a cheap fingerprint check
(record count, failed record identities, registration count, share-store shape),
so a full collect only runs when the fingerprint changes. A module rejection
refreshes diagnostics even when no new module has arrived. Ordinary stage
advancement still waits for the next fingerprint change or a manual refresh.

## Architecture

The UI renders a plain, structured-clone-safe `Snapshot` and never touches a
live loader object. That one constraint is what makes a devtools extension a
packaging exercise rather than a rewrite — in an extension the panel runs in a
different realm and only JSON can cross.

```
core/        collectors + Snapshot model      no DOM, no framework
analysis/    graph, share resolution, issues  pure functions over a Snapshot
adapters/    LiveAdapter | RemoteAdapter      same interface, either realm
ui/          Preact + signals in a Shadow DOM renders a Snapshot, nothing else
```

Everything it needs is compiled into the drop-in: Preact, signals and the ELK
layout engine. Nothing is imported through the page's SystemJS or federation,
nothing is fetched at runtime, and no module is registered with the loader —
an observer that participated in what it observes would be reporting on
itself. (This is why ELK's *bundled* build is used rather than its worker
build, which fetches `elk-worker.js` on first layout.)

`adapters/remote.ts` ships both ends of a `postMessage` bridge:
`serveRemote(transport)` in a content script, `new RemoteAdapter(transport)` in
a devtools panel, and the existing UI on top of it unchanged.

## Development

```sh
fyn            # install
fyn run build  # tsc + rollup + terser -> dist/
fyn run test   # vitest
```

Outputs:

| File | Format | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dist/federation-inspector.js` | IIFE, Preact bundled in | the drop-in |
| `dist/federation-inspector.min.js` | IIFE, minified | production drop-in |
| `dist/index.js` | ESM, Preact external | library / extension |
| `dist/*.d.ts` | — | types |

Design notes: [`../../notes/federation-inspector-design.md`](https://github.com/jchip/fynmesh/blob/main/notes/federation-inspector-design.md).

# Run Multiple React Versions on One Page

URL: https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/run-multiple-react-versions

Yes, you can run React 18 and React 19 micro frontends on the same page. In FynMesh each FynApp declares the React range it accepts. The federation runtime shares one copy per compatible range, so apps that agree share a copy and a new major gets its own.

This is the main thing FynMesh does differently. Most setups force one React for the whole page. FynMesh lets each app keep the version it was built for.

## How it works

A FynApp is an independently built and deployed micro frontend. Its build writes a manifest that lists what it provides and what it consumes. The kernel reads that manifest before it runs the app.

Two pieces do the sharing:

- `rollup-plugin-federation` builds a container for each FynApp. The container declares each shared module and the semver range it accepts.
- `federation-js` runs in the browser. It picks a loaded version that satisfies the range, and loads another copy when nothing fits.

All FynApps on a page join one share scope named `fynmesh`. Nobody lists their peers. Apps that land on the page together share code automatically.

## The provider side

A provider is a FynApp that ships a shared module. The demo has two React providers. Both are named `fynapp-react-lib`. They differ only in version and range.

The React 19 provider, from `demo/fynapp-react-19/rollup.config.ts`:

```ts
...setupFederationPlugins({
  name: "fynapp-react-lib",
  exposes: {},
  shared: {
    "esm-react": { singleton: false, semver: "^19.0.0" },
    "esm-react-dom": { singleton: false, semver: "^19.0.0" },
  },
}),
```

The React 18 provider in `demo/fynapp-react-18` is the same file with `^18.0.0`. The demo uses the `esm-react` and `esm-react-dom` packages, which are ESM builds of React. A project of your own uses the standard `react` and `react-dom` packages instead.

`setupFederationPlugins` comes from the `create-fynapp` package. It wraps `rollup-plugin-federation` and sets the share scope, entry file name and manifest hooks for you.

## The consumer side

A consumer is a FynApp that uses React but does not bundle it. The app `fynapp-1` runs React 19. Its `package.json` depends on the provider range:

```json
"dependencies": {
  "fynapp-react-lib": "^19.0.0"
}
```

Its build then records the need in `dist/fynapp.manifest.json`:

```json
"consume-shared": {
  "esm-react": { "semver": "^19.0.0" },
  "esm-react-dom": { "semver": "^19.0.0" }
},
"shared-providers": {
  "fynapp-react-lib": {
    "semver": "^19.0.0",
    "provides": ["esm-react", "esm-react-dom"]
  }
}
```

The kernel reads `shared-providers` to know which provider to load first. The consumer then resolves `esm-react` against the range `^19.0.0`.

The app `fynapp-2-react18` is different. It provides its own React 18 through the shared config, with `semver: "^18.0.0"`. So the page ends up with a React 18 copy from that app and a React 19 copy from `fynapp-react-lib`.

## What is shared and what is not

The share scope holds one module instance per resolved copy. That has clear consequences.

Shared, when ranges agree:

- Three React 19 apps load one `react` 19 copy. They share its hooks dispatcher and its context.
- The download happens once.

Not shared, across versions:

- React 18 and React 19 are separate module instances. They do not see each other's state.
- A React context created in a 19 app is invisible to a component rendered by 18.
- A component tree must not mix elements from the two copies.

Treat each version as a separate island. Pass data between islands as plain values, through the kernel's middleware or through a small store that does not depend on React.

## Why `singleton` is false

Look again at the provider config. Both providers set `singleton: false`. This matters.

A singleton share means one copy for the whole scope. Once any version is in play, every consumer resolves to it, even a consumer whose range excludes it. The runtime only prints a warning. That is the right choice for libraries that must be unique. It is the wrong choice when you want React 18 and React 19 side by side.

So for React, `singleton: false` is what allows two majors to coexist. The next guide, [share dependencies by semver range](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/share-dependencies-semver), covers the rules in more detail.

## Two versions of the same app

The same idea works for your own FynApps, not only for React. The demo has `fynapp-x1` in two versions, built from `demo/fynapp-x1-v1` and `demo/fynapp-x1-v2`. Both have the name `fynapp-x1`. They have versions 1.0.0 and 2.0.0.

The v1 build shares React 18 and does not bundle it:

```ts
shared: {
  "esm-react": { import: false, singleton: false, semver: "^18.3.0" },
  "esm-react-dom": { import: false, singleton: false, semver: "^18.3.0" },
},
```

The v2 build uses the React 19 helper. Consumers pick a version with a range in the import:

```ts
import("fynapp-x1/main", { with: { type: "mf-expose", semver: "^2.0.0" } })
```

In the demo, `fynapp-2-react18` asks for `^1.0.0`. The apps `fynapp-1` and `fynapp-1-b` ask for `^2.0.0`. All three run on one page. Each gets the version that fits its range. The same page loads one name at two majors.

## Check what the page decided

The federation inspector shows which copy each app got. Open its Shares tab and look for the two `esm-react` entries. The Issues tab flags two copies of a singleton. See the [federation inspector docs](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/federation-inspector) for setup.

## Try it

- Open the [live demo](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/demo) and find `fynapp-1` (React 19) and `fynapp-2-react18` (React 18) on the same page.
- Read the [same app, multiple versions section](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/features#versions) and the [semver sharing section](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/features#shared) on the features page.
- Read how the loader resolves ranges in the [federation-js docs](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/federation-js).
- Read [how to upgrade React one micro frontend at a time](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/upgrade-react-incrementally).

---

# Share Dependencies Across Micro Frontends by Semver

URL: https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/share-dependencies-semver

Each FynApp declares the shared modules it uses and the semver range it accepts. At runtime `federation-js` picks a loaded version that satisfies that range. If none fits, it falls back to loading a copy of its own.

This guide covers the config, how a range picks a version, what `singleton` changes, and how to see the result.

## Declare a shared module

Sharing is configured in the Rollup build through `rollup-plugin-federation`. The `shared` option maps a module name to its config:

```js
import federation from "rollup-plugin-federation";

federation({
  name: "plugin_1",
  filename: "federation-entry.js",
  exposes: { "./bootstrap": "./src/bootstrap.js" },
  shared: {
    react: { singleton: true, semver: "^19.0.0" },
  },
});
```

The fields that matter:

- `semver` is the range this container accepts.
- `singleton` asks for one instance across all containers.
- `import` says whether to bundle a copy, or treat the module as external.

A module used only through another package still has to appear in `shared` with its range. Listing it as an external is not enough. The failure shows up at runtime as a duplicate instance, not as a build error.

In a FynApp you rarely call the plugin directly. The `create-fynapp` helpers wrap it. This is the React 18 config of `fynapp-2-react18` in the demo:

```ts
...setupFederationPlugins({
  name: "fynapp-2-react18",
  exposes: {
    "./main": "./src/main.ts",
    "./App": "./src/App.tsx",
    "./component": "./src/component.ts",
  },
  shared: {
    "esm-react": { singleton: false, semver: "^18.0.0" },
    "esm-react-dom": { singleton: false, semver: "^18.0.0" },
  },
}),
```

## What the build records

The build writes `dist/fynapp.manifest.json`. It is embedded in the entry file too, so the kernel reads it without an extra request. Two fields describe sharing.

An app that provides a module lists it under `provide-shared`:

```json
"provide-shared": {
  "esm-react": { "singleton": false, "semver": "^18.0.0" }
}
```

An app that needs a module lists it under `consume-shared`, and names which FynApp provides it under `shared-providers`:

```json
"consume-shared": { "esm-react": { "semver": "^19.0.0" } },
"shared-providers": {
  "fynapp-react-lib": { "semver": "^19.0.0", "provides": ["esm-react", "esm-react-dom"] }
}
```

The provider comes from the consumer's `package.json` dependency. In `fynapp-1`, that is `"fynapp-react-lib": "^19.0.0"`. Build order matters here. The consumer's build reads the provider's manifest off disk, so build providers first.

## How a range picks a version

When code imports a shared module, the runtime resolves it in this order:

1. Look for a version that is already loaded and satisfies the consumer's range.
2. If none is loaded, look for a registered but not yet loaded version that satisfies it.
3. If nothing in the share scope fits, resolve the import the ordinary way, which loads the copy the consumer ships.

Take three apps in one scope. Two ask for `^19.0.0` and one asks for `^18.0.0`. The first two get one shared React 19 copy. The third gets a React 18 copy. Nobody had to coordinate.

You can also pick a version of an exposed module. A consumer writes the range in the import itself:

```ts
import("fynapp-x1/main", { with: { type: "mf-expose", semver: "^2.0.0" } })
```

The page then picks the loaded `fynapp-x1` version that fits. This is how `fynapp-x1` 1.0.0 and 2.0.0 live on one demo page.

## Singleton and non-singleton

The two modes answer different needs.

A non-singleton share (`singleton: false`) follows the rules above. Different ranges can produce different copies. Use it when two majors must coexist, such as React 18 and 19.

A singleton share means one copy for the whole scope. Once any version is in play, every consumer gets that version. A consumer whose range excludes it still gets it, and the runtime logs a warning that names the container. It does not throw. Refusing the import would break a page that otherwise works, and the fix belongs in the app's declared range.

Use a singleton when two copies would be a bug. Libraries that keep global state or a registry fit here. Two copies of a library like that cause failures such as an invalid hook call.

Pick by asking one question. Can two versions of this module safely run side by side? If yes, use `false`. If no, use `true`.

The scaffold for a new React FynApp from `create-fynapp` uses singleton shares for `react`, `react-dom` and `react-dom/client`. That suits a page with one React major. For two majors, set `singleton: false` as the demo providers do.

## When no compatible version exists

For a non-singleton share, the consumer falls back to its own copy. That keeps the page working. The cost is a second copy of the module.

For a singleton share, there is no second copy once a version has loaded. The loaded version wins, and you get the warning. Watch the browser console for the line that says the module "is declared singleton".

Both outcomes are visible in the inspector. Fix them by widening the consumer's range, or by upgrading the app that is behind.

## See it in the federation inspector

The federation inspector is a script tag that adds a badge to the page. Click it to open a panel. It answers the questions that browser devtools cannot:

- Who shares `esm-react`, at which versions, and from where?
- Which copy did each app get, and does its range allow that copy?
- Are there two copies of a singleton in play?

Use the Shares tab to see each share key with its versions. Use the Issues tab to find duplicate singletons and failed loads. Setup is in the [federation inspector docs](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/federation-inspector).

For a minified page, `Federation.__I()` returns a snapshot of the resolution decisions. It lists the declared ranges and the ranges that were applied. The [federation-js docs](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/federation-js) describe it.

## Next steps

- Watch semver sharing on the [live demo](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/demo) and read the [features page](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/features#shared).
- Read how [two React versions share a page](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/run-multiple-react-versions).
- Read [how to upgrade React one micro frontend at a time](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/upgrade-react-incrementally).
- Read the options table in the [rollup-plugin-federation docs](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/rollup-plugin-federation).

---

# Upgrade React One Micro Frontend at a Time

URL: https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/upgrade-react-incrementally

You can upgrade React one micro frontend at a time. FynMesh runs React 18 and React 19 apps on the same page, so old apps stay on 18 while new ones move to 19. Each team changes its own app and ships when it is ready. There is no big-bang upgrade day.

This guide gives a step-by-step plan and the pitfalls to watch for.

## Why a big-bang upgrade hurts

With one shared React, every app on the page must move together. One blocked team blocks everyone. A rollback means reverting every app.

FynMesh removes that coupling. Each FynApp declares the React range it accepts. The runtime shares one copy per compatible range. The [first guide](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/run-multiple-react-versions) explains how that works.

## The plan

### 1. Set a baseline

List your FynApps and note the React range each one uses. Open the page with the [federation inspector](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/federation-inspector) and look at the Shares tab. You should see one `react` entry per major.

### 2. Add a React 19 provider

A provider is a FynApp that ships React for others to consume. The demo has one per major, both named `fynapp-react-lib`. The React 19 one declares:

```ts
shared: {
  "esm-react": { singleton: false, semver: "^19.0.0" },
  "esm-react-dom": { singleton: false, semver: "^19.0.0" },
},
```

Your existing React 18 provider stays as it is. Both providers can be live on the page at once. The demo uses `esm-react` packages. In your own project the names are `react` and `react-dom`.

### 3. Keep the shares non-singleton

Set `singleton: false` on React in every provider. A singleton React forces every consumer onto one copy and only warns when a range does not fit. That defeats the point. The [semver guide](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/share-dependencies-semver) covers the rules.

### 4. Upgrade the leaf apps first

Pick an app that nobody else imports from. Change its dependency to the new provider:

```json
"dependencies": {
  "fynapp-react-lib": "^19.0.0"
}
```

Update its React types and code, then build it. Its manifest now says `consume-shared` with `^19.0.0`, and `shared-providers` points at the 19 provider. The other apps do not change.

In the demo, `fynapp-1` is a React 19 app next to `fynapp-2-react18`, which stays on React 18. They share a page and ship separately.

### 5. Check the page

Load the page and open the inspector. You should see two React copies, one per major. The Issues tab should show no duplicate singletons. Watch the console for singleton warnings.

### 6. Deploy that one app

Ship the upgraded app on its own. The other apps are untouched. If something breaks, roll back that one app.

### 7. Repeat, then retire the old provider

Move the next app. When no app consumes the React 18 provider, remove it. The page then loads one React copy again, and nothing else changed.

## Shared FynApps need versions too

Some FynApps are shared between apps, like a component library. Upgrading them is a two version job. The demo's `fynapp-x1` ships 1.0.0 on React 18 and 2.0.0 on React 19. Both are live.

Consumers pick with a range:

```ts
import("fynapp-x1/main", { with: { type: "mf-expose", semver: "^2.0.0" } })
```

In the demo, `fynapp-2-react18` asks for `^1.0.0`. The apps `fynapp-1` and `fynapp-1-b` ask for `^2.0.0`. A library team can ship 2.0.0 and let consumers move when they choose.

## Legacy RequireJS bundles

Older micro frontends built as webpack AMD bundles can follow the same plan. They get React from federation through a FynApp that serves their common libraries, with no rebuild, and move to a new major one RequireJS context at a time. See [Serve shared libraries to legacy RequireJS bundles](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/legacy-requirejs-on-module-federation).

## Pitfalls

### State and context do not cross versions

React 18 and 19 are separate module instances. A context made in a 19 app is invisible to an 18 component. Hooks from one copy do not work in a tree rendered by the other.

Do not pass React elements or hooks across the boundary. Pass plain data. Use middleware or a store that does not depend on React for cross-app state.

### Singleton libraries

A library that must be unique, such as a store or a router with global state, should be a singleton share. If two apps on different React majors both use it, the singleton keeps one copy. Check that this one copy works with both React versions. If it does not, upgrade or isolate it first.

### Ranges that do not match

If a consumer's range excludes every loaded version and the share is a singleton, the loaded version wins and the runtime logs a warning. The app may then run against a React it was not built for. Fix the range, not the warning.

### Build order

A consumer's build reads its provider's manifest from disk. Build providers before consumers. If you build in the wrong order, the consumer's `shared-providers` field comes out empty.

### The scaffold defaults

The `create-fynapp` scaffold for React uses singleton shares for `react`, `react-dom` and `react-dom/client`. That suits a page with one React major. Set `singleton: false` on the providers when you want two majors during a migration.

## Rollout summary

| Step | Who | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add React 19 provider | Platform team | Two providers live |
| Upgrade one leaf app | App team | One app on 19 |
| Check in inspector | App team | Two copies, no issues |
| Deploy that app | App team | Others untouched |
| Repeat | Each team | Old provider unused |
| Remove React 18 provider | Platform team | One copy again |

## Try it

- Open the [live demo](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/demo) to see `fynapp-1` on React 19 and `fynapp-2-react18` on React 18.
- Read [how multiple React versions run on one page](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/run-multiple-react-versions).
- Read [how legacy RequireJS bundles get React from federation](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/legacy-requirejs-on-module-federation).
- Read [how semver ranges choose a version](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/share-dependencies-semver).
- Read the [FynApp contract](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/fynapp-contract) and the [kernel docs](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/kernel).

# Serve Shared Libraries to Legacy RequireJS Bundles from Module Federation

URL: https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/legacy-requirejs-on-module-federation

Before Module Federation, many micro frontends were built on RequireJS. Each widget is an AMD bundle. Shared libraries are built into a common web package (CWP), and widgets consume it through webpack externals. FynMesh can serve the CWP's libraries to those widgets from federation, under the ids they already ask for, with no rebuild. A codebase can then move to federation progressively.

This guide explains the setup, what changes, and what you get. The working code is in the [live demo](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/legacy-amd).

## The legacy setup

In a RequireJS micro frontend, each widget is built with webpack as an AMD bundle. A platform team builds the shared libraries, like React and the UI kit, into a common web package (CWP). Widgets list those libraries as webpack externals. In the built file, each external becomes a RequireJS dependency that the CWP provides:

```js
define(["react", "react-dom", "ui-kit"], function (React, ReactDOM, UIKit) { ... });
```

## The problem

A large enterprise builds up many widgets from many teams over time, and they all depend on the same CWP. Updating a library version or adding a variant means every team must move together. At that scale it is near impossible.

Module Federation solves version sharing, but legacy AMD widgets cannot use it. A large codebase also cannot migrate all its widgets in one shot. It needs a way to introduce federation progressively. The bridge below gives it one: legacy widgets and FynApps run on the same page, and the codebase moves over one piece at a time.

## What changes

Two pieces connect the legacy bundles to federation:

- **The CWP becomes a FynApp.** It installs the same libraries at the same pinned versions. It shares them through federation, and it publishes which RequireJS ids it serves.
- **A kernel add-on routes RequireJS to it.** When a bundle asks for `react` or `ui-kit`, the add-on loads it from the CWP FynApp. Every other id, such as the bundles themselves, loads through RequireJS as before.

The legacy bundles and the page's RequireJS setup stay as they are. The add-on and the CWP's id list are added to the page before the first `require()`.

## What you get

- **No rebuild.** The same bundle files run on the federated libraries.
- **Upgrades in stages.** Each RequireJS context chooses the legacy CWP or the federated one. One group of widgets can move to a CWP release with React 19 while another stays on the legacy CWP with React 18.
- **One React for old and new apps.** New FynApps on the same page share the CWP's React when their version range matches. A FynApp that needs another major loads its own.
- **On-demand loading.** A bundle loaded later reuses the libraries its context already has.

## Moving to a new React major

1. Release a CWP FynApp that pins the libraries the legacy CWP had. Point one RequireJS context at it and check that its widgets behave the same.
2. Move the other contexts over one at a time. A context you have not moved stays on the legacy CWP.
3. Release a CWP with the new React major, and point the federated contexts at it. The widgets are not rebuilt.
4. Retire the legacy CWP once no context uses it.

React 19 removed `ReactDOM.render`, `findDOMNode`, string refs and `propTypes`. A legacy widget that uses them needs a code change before it can run on React 19. Widgets that use `createRoot` run on both majors.

## Limits

- A page runs one federated CWP release. Every federated context on the page uses it. Other contexts stay on the legacy CWP.
- The CWP's id list must load before the first `require()`.
- The AMD add-on is a working prototype in the FynMesh repo, in `demo-legacy-amd/`. It is not a published package yet.

## Try it

- Open the [legacy RequireJS demo](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/legacy-amd). Put each set of widgets on the legacy or the federated CWP, with React 18 or React 19.
- Read [Upgrade React one micro frontend at a time](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/upgrade-react-incrementally) for the same plan with FynApps.
- Read [how kernel add-ons work](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/how-it-works#8-kernel-add-ons).

---

# Build Micro Frontends with Rollup

URL: https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/micro-frontends-with-rollup

FynMesh builds each micro frontend with Rollup. We call one a FynApp. The `rollup-plugin-federation` plugin turns a Rollup build into a federated container, and the FynMesh kernel loads that container in the browser by name.

You do not need webpack. A FynApp is a normal Rollup project with one extra plugin and one exported object.

## What you build

A FynApp has three parts.

- `rollup.config.ts` names the app, lists what it exposes and what it shares.
- `src/main.ts` exports `main`, the entry the kernel runs.
- `dist/` holds the build: `fynapp-entry.js` and `fynapp.manifest.json`.

Each FynApp is built and deployed on its own. The host page only needs the kernel and the app's name.

## Scaffold a FynApp

Install the CLI with fyn, then create an app.

```bash
fyn global add create-fynapp
create-fynapp --name my-app --framework react
```

The `--framework` flag accepts `react`, `react18`, `preact`, `vue`, `solid`, `svelte`, `marko` and `vanilla`. These eight have full templates. Any other name gets a generic skeleton that builds as is and comes with an `AGENT-TODO.md` checklist.

The command writes `package.json`, `tsconfig.json`, `rollup.config.ts` and starter sources. Use `--skip-install` if you want the files without the install step.

## The Rollup config

Most apps use the `createFynAppRollupConfig` factory from `create-fynapp`.

```ts
import { createFynAppRollupConfig } from "create-fynapp";

export default createFynAppRollupConfig({
  name: "example-vanilla",
  framework: "vanilla",
  typescript: true,
  exposes: {
    "./main": "./src/main.ts",
  },
});
```

For `framework: "react"` the factory adds the `./main` expose for you. Every other framework must list it. The factory emits SystemJS output into `dist/` and assembles the Rollup plugins in a fixed order, with the federation plugin among them.

Under the hood this calls `rollup-plugin-federation`. Its main options are:

- `name`: the container name. Required.
- `filename`: the container entry file. It must also appear in Rollup's `input`.
- `exposes`: modules other apps can load, as `{ "./main": "./src/main.ts" }`.
- `shared`: modules shared at runtime, each with `singleton` and a `semver` range.

The Vue demo app shows the lower-level form. It exposes `./main` and shares `vue` as a singleton.

```ts
...setupFederationPlugins({
  name: "fynapp-4-vue",
  exposes: {
    "./main": "./src/main.js",
  },
  shared: {
    vue: {
      singleton: true,
      semver: "^3.3.4",
    },
  },
}),
```

See the [rollup-plugin-federation docs](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/rollup-plugin-federation) for every option.

## Build it

Inside a FynApp, run Rollup through the `cfa` command or the package script.

```bash
cfa build
cfa build --watch
cfa check
```

`cfa check` builds the app and confirms that `dist/fynapp-entry.js` and a valid `dist/fynapp.manifest.json` exist. The manifest lists the app's name, exposes and shared modules. The same manifest is embedded in `fynapp-entry.js`, so the kernel reads it without an extra request.

Build order matters when apps depend on each other. An app that consumes a shared module reads its provider's manifest from disk at build time. Build the provider first.

## Write the FynUnit

`src/main.ts` exports `main`. This object is a FynUnit. Only `execute` is required. `initialize` is optional and runs first.

```ts
import { useMiddleware } from "@fynmesh/kernel";
import type { FynUnit, FynUnitRuntime } from "@fynmesh/kernel";

class VanillaUnit implements FynUnit {
  initialize(_runtime: FynUnitRuntime) {
    return { status: "ready", mode: "standalone" };
  }

  execute(runtime: FynUnitRuntime) {
    const target = document.createElement("div");
    target.textContent = `Hello from ${runtime.fynApp.name}`;
    document.body.appendChild(target);
  }
}

export const main = useMiddleware([], new VanillaUnit());
```

`main` can also be a plain object with `execute`, or a bare function. The kernel wraps a function as `{ execute: fn }`. The [FynApp contract](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/fynapp-contract) lists the other lifecycle methods: `shutdown`, `suspend` and `resume`.

## Load it in a host page

The host page loads three scripts: SystemJS, `federation-js` and the browser kernel. The kernel then loads apps by name.

```html
<script src="/system.min.js"></script>
<script src="/federation-js/dist/federation-js.min.js"></script>
<script src="/kernel/dist/fynmesh-browser-kernel.min.js"></script>
<script>
  fynMeshKernel.loadFynAppsByName([
    { name: "fynapp-1" },
    { name: "fynapp-4-vue" },
  ]);
</script>
```

The kernel resolves each name through a registry resolver. The demo maps a name to `/<name>/dist/fynapp.manifest.json`. You set your own mapping with `fynMeshKernel.setRegistryResolver(async (name, range) => ({ name, version, url, distBase }))`.

`loadFynAppsByName` reads the manifests, builds a dependency graph, and loads apps in dependency order. Independent apps load in parallel, four at a time by default. A failed app does not stop the others.

## React, Vue, Preact, Solid, Svelte and Marko

The Rollup setup is the same for every framework. Only the framework plugin and the shared package change.

- React: `createFynAppRollupConfig` with `framework: "react"`. React, React DOM and `react-dom/client` are shared singletons.
- Vue: `vue` shared with `^3.3.4`.
- Preact: `fynapp-5-preact` shares Preact as a singleton.
- Solid: `solid-js` shared with `^1.9.15`.
- Svelte: `fynapp-8-svelte` shares Svelte as a singleton.
- Marko: `fynapp-3-marko` shares Marko as a singleton.

The [live demo](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/demo) loads all six on one page. Each app is built and loaded on its own. The source for each is under `demo/` in the repository.

## Why Rollup

Production builds run through terser and emit no sourcemaps by default. Many small chunks can be folded into fewer files with `federation-combine`, a post-build step in `rollup-plugin-federation`. The federation output format here is SystemJS, which `federation-js` loads at runtime.

## Try it

- Open the [live demo](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/demo) to see six frameworks on one page.
- Try the [shell demo](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/shell) to see apps composed through middleware.
- Read [Getting Started](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/getting-started) for the full scaffolder reference.
- Learn how loading works in the [kernel docs](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/kernel).
- See how federation works without webpack in [Module Federation Without Webpack](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/module-federation-without-webpack).
- Run two versions of one library in [Run Multiple React Versions on One Page](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/run-multiple-react-versions).

---

# Module Federation Without Webpack

URL: https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/module-federation-without-webpack

FynMesh provides Module Federation for Rollup builds. The `rollup-plugin-federation` plugin builds the containers, and the `federation-js` runtime wires them together in the browser. It is based on SystemJS, so you do not need webpack.

On top of that, the FynMesh kernel loads apps by name and version, boots them in dependency order, and can run several versions of the same app on one page.

## The pieces

There are four pieces. Each has one job.

- Build plugin: `rollup-plugin-federation` generates a container for your build.
- Container entry: the file the plugin emits. It lists what the build exposes and shares.
- Runtime: `federation-js` loads containers and resolves shared modules in the browser.
- Share scope: a named namespace where containers register what they share.

The build and the runtime are separate packages. Build output does not need the build tool at runtime.

## The build plugin

Add the plugin to a Rollup config. `filename` names the container entry, and it must also be listed in `input`.

```js
import federation from "rollup-plugin-federation";

export default {
  input: ["src/index.js", "federation-entry.js"],
  output: { dir: "dist", format: "esm" },
  plugins: [
    federation({
      name: "plugin_1",
      filename: "federation-entry.js",
      exposes: {
        "./bootstrap": "./src/bootstrap.js",
      },
      shared: {
        react: { singleton: true, semver: "^19.0.0" },
      },
    }),
  ],
};
```

The plugin collects shared modules and their importers. It emits the container code and a `federation.json` file that records exposes, chunks and share config. The runtime does not need `federation.json`, because the entry file carries the container.

Each `shared` entry takes a semver range and a few flags: `singleton`, `eager` and `import`. A dependency used only through another package still needs a `shared` entry with its range. Otherwise a mismatch shows up at runtime as a duplicate instance, not as a build error.

When a build has many small exposes, `federation-combine` folds the small chunks into fewer files after the build.

## The runtime

`federation-js` expects a `System` global. It must be the SystemJS fork that ships in the same package, not stock SystemJS. Load the loader first, then the runtime.

```html
<script src="/node_modules/federation-js/dist/system.min.js"></script>
<script src="/node_modules/federation-js/dist/federation-js.min.js"></script>
```

Importing the runtime installs a global `Federation` object. You can load a container and ask it for an exposed module.

```js
Federation.import("__mf_container_plugin_1")
  .then((container) => container.get("./bootstrap"))
  .then((getModule) => console.log("module", getModule()));
```

A shared module is fetched the same way, by the name it was shared under.

```js
Federation.import("__mf_container_plugin_1")
  .then((container) => container.get("react"));
```

## Output format

The plugin example above uses ESM output to stay short. FynApps built with `create-fynapp` emit SystemJS output instead, because `federation-js` registers modules through the SystemJS loader. The `createFynAppRollupConfig` factory sets this for you, along with the share scope name `fynmesh`.

## How a container is loaded

A container is a script. When it runs, it registers its name, its version, its exposes and its shared modules with the runtime. Asking for an expose runs the module's code once, on first import.

Several modules can also ship in one physical file. Each still registers under its own name, so importing it looks the same. The runtime fetches the file once, however many members ask for it.

## How sharing works at runtime

Each container declares the semver range it accepts for every shared module. The runtime looks at the versions already loaded in the share scope and picks one that satisfies the range. If nothing matches, the container loads its own copy.

A container that only consumes a shared module can still resolve it, as long as a container that shares it has already loaded. Singletons keep one instance across containers.

`Federation.__I()` returns a snapshot of what the runtime decided for each share key. It is the main tool for debugging a minified page. The [federation inspector](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/federation-inspector) reads this kind of information for you.

## What FynMesh adds on top

The plugin and runtime are the Module Federation layer. The kernel is the layer above it.

- Load by name and semver. `fynMeshKernel.loadFynAppsByName([{ name: "fynapp-x1", range: "^2.0.0" }])` resolves the name through a registry resolver you provide.
- Dependency ordered boot. The kernel reads each app's manifest, builds a graph from `requires`, `import-exposed` and `shared-providers`, and loads providers before their consumers.
- Middleware. An app can use middleware published by another app, such as a shared layout or design tokens.
- Several versions of the same app. The demo ships `fynapp-react-lib` as both a React 18 and a React 19 app. It also ships `fynapp-x1` in two versions. The kernel keeps them apart and gives each consumer the one its range asks for.
- Error isolation. A failed app emits an event and does not crash the others.

Here is a host page that loads two apps by name.

```html
<script src="/system.min.js"></script>
<script src="/federation-js/dist/federation-js.min.js"></script>
<script src="/kernel/dist/fynmesh-browser-kernel.min.js"></script>
<script>
  fynMeshKernel.loadFynAppsByName([
    { name: "fynapp-1" },
    { name: "fynapp-4-vue" },
  ]);
</script>
```

## Compared with webpack

Webpack ships its own Module Federation plugin and its own runtime, tied to the webpack build. FynMesh keeps the same idea but moves it to Rollup. The runtime is `federation-js` on a SystemJS style registry, not the webpack runtime. Pick based on the bundler your apps already use.

- Watch the [live demo](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/demo) load six frameworks on one page.
- Read the [rollup-plugin-federation docs](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/rollup-plugin-federation) for all plugin options.
- Read the [federation-js docs](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/federation-js) for the runtime.
- Read the [kernel docs](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/docs/kernel) for loading, middleware and lifecycle.
- Follow [Build Micro Frontends with Rollup](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/micro-frontends-with-rollup) to build your first app.
- See [Share Dependencies with Semver](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/share-dependencies-semver) for share rules in depth.
- See [Run Multiple React Versions on One Page](https://www.fynmesh.fyi/guides/run-multiple-react-versions) for the multi-version case.
